section.title: Ananias and Sapphira and the Apostles Persecuted
section.sectionRationale: Set against the shining generosity that closed chapter 4, this chapter opens with a lie at the heart of the church: Ananias and Sapphira pretend to give everything while secretly keeping back part of the price, and God strikes them down, so that great fear falls on the church. Then the apostles heal many, are arrested by the jealous high priest, freed by an angel, and hauled again before the Sanhedrin, where they declare they must obey God rather than men and testify to the risen and exalted Christ. Gamaliel's cautious counsel spares their lives; they are flogged, and they leave rejoicing to have suffered for the Name.
section.thesis: The holy God who fills His church with His Spirit will not be lied to or trifled with, and the same risen Christ whom He has exalted as Prince and Savior gives His witnesses a courage that outlasts prison, angelic rescue, threats, and flogging, so that the persecuted apostles rejoice to suffer for the Name and never stop proclaiming that Jesus is the Christ.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the deadly deceit of Ananias and Sapphira; the healing power and growth of the church; the arrest of the apostles and their release by an angel; their bold testimony before the council that they must obey God rather than men; and Gamaliel's counsel, the flogging, and the apostles' joy in suffering for the Name.

units.label: The deadly deceit of Ananias and Sapphira
units.note: a lie to the Holy Spirit, and great fear falls on the church

verses.text: Now a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, also sold a piece of property.
With his wife’s full knowledge, he {{nosphizomai|kept back}} some of the proceeds for himself, but brought a portion and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
Then Peter said, “Ananias, how is it that Satan has filled your heart to {{pseudomai|lie}} to the Holy Spirit and withhold some of the proceeds from the land?
Did it not belong to you before it was sold? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? How could you conceive such a deed in your heart? You have not lied to men, but to God!”
On hearing these words, Ananias fell down and died. And great fear came over all who heard what had happened.
Then the young men stepped forward, wrapped up his body, and carried him out and buried him.
About three hours later his wife also came in, unaware of what had happened.
“Tell me,” said Peter, “is this the price you and your husband got for the land?” “Yes,” she answered, “that is the price.”
“How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?” Peter replied. “Look, the feet of the men who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out also.”
At that instant she fell down at his feet and died. Then the young men came in and, finding her dead, carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
And great fear came over the whole church and all who heard about these events.

units.label: Signs and wonders, and the church grows
units.note: the sick are healed and multitudes are added to the Lord

verses.text: The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people, and with one accord the believers gathered together in Solomon’s Colonnade.
Although the people regarded them highly, no one else dared to join them.
Yet more and more believers were brought to the Lord, large numbers of both men and women.
As a result, people brought the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passed by.
Crowds also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and all of them were healed.

units.label: Arrested and freed by night
units.note: jealousy imprisons the apostles, but an angel opens the doors

verses.text: Then the high priest and all his associates, who belonged to the party of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy. They went out
and arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail.
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out, saying,
“Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.”

At daybreak the apostles entered the temple courts as they had been told and began to teach the people. When the high priest and his associates arrived, they convened the Sanhedrin, the full assembly of the elders of Israel, and sent to the jail for the apostles.
But on arriving at the jail, the officers did not find them there. So they returned with the report:
“We found the jail securely locked, with the guards posted at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside.”
When the captain of the temple guard and the chief priests heard this account, they were perplexed as to what was happening.
Then someone came in and announced, “Look, the men you put in jail are standing in the temple courts teaching the people!”
At that point, the captain went with the officers and brought the apostles, but not by force, for fear the people would stone them.

units.label: We must obey God rather than men
units.note: the exalted Prince and Savior grants repentance to Israel

verses.text: They brought them in and made them stand before the Sanhedrin, where the high priest interrogated them.
“We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name,” he said. “Yet you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and are determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood.”
But Peter and the other apostles replied, “We must {{peitharcheo|obey}} God rather than men.
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree.
God exalted Him to His right hand as {{archegos|Prince}} and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel.
We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him.”

units.label: Gamaliel's counsel, the flogging, and joy in the Name
units.note: if it is from God you cannot stop it; the apostles rejoice to suffer

verses.text: When the Council members heard this, they were enraged, and they resolved to put the apostles to death.
But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law who was honored by all the people, stood up in the Sanhedrin and ordered that the men be put outside for a short time.
“Men of Israel,” he said, “consider carefully what you are about to do to these men.
Some time ago Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and about four hundred men joined him. He was killed, all his followers were dispersed, and it all came to nothing.
After him, Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census and drew away people after him. He too perished, and all his followers were scattered.
So in the present case I advise you: Leave these men alone. Let them go! For if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail.
But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.”
At this, they yielded to Gamaliel. They called the apostles in and had them flogged. Then they ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them.
The apostles left the Sanhedrin, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name.
Every day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ.

nosphizomai.gloss: To set apart secretly for oneself, to embezzle or pilfer, to keep back part of what should be handed over. The Greek Old Testament uses this very word for Achan, who kept back some of the devoted things at Jericho, Joshua 7. The echo is deliberate: like Achan, Ananias secretly withholds while pretending full surrender, and the sin brings death into the camp of God's holy people.

pseudomai.gloss: To lie, to speak falsehood, to deceive. Peter names the true nature of the couple's act: it was not a mere financial reservation but a lie, and a lie aimed not merely at the apostles but at the Holy Spirit and at God Himself. The sin was hypocrisy, staging a total gift to win praise while the heart held back, and pretending before the God who sees the heart.

peitharcheo.gloss: To obey a ruling authority, to submit to and follow orders. The apostles use it to state a settled principle: they must obey God rather than men. When the command of any human authority collides with the clear command of God, the Christian's higher allegiance is to God; obedience to Him is not rebellion but the deepest loyalty, and it may cost dearly.

archegos.gloss: Leader, originator, pioneer, prince; the one who goes first and opens the way for others to follow. God has exalted the crucified Jesus to His right hand as Archegos and Savior. He is the trailblazer of life, the founder of a new humanity, who leads His people through death into resurrection, and from His throne He grants repentance and forgiveness to Israel.

basic.context: Chapter 4 ended with the church's beautiful generosity and Barnabas laying his gift at the apostles' feet. Now Ananias and Sapphira imitate the outward act but with a lie underneath: they sell property, secretly keep part of the price, yet pretend to give it all. Peter exposes the deceit as a lie to the Holy Spirit, and both fall dead, so that great fear grips the church. Then the apostles heal many and are arrested by the jealous high priest, freed by an angel, and brought again before the council, where they refuse to stop preaching Jesus. Gamaliel urges caution, they are flogged, and they rejoice to suffer for the Name.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the Ananias story not as God punishing generosity but as God guarding the holiness and truthfulness of His new community at a foundational moment. The point is not the size of the gift but the lie. Then read the trial scenes as another round in the pattern begun in chapter 4: witness, arrest, deliverance, testimony, threat, and joy. The apostles' words in verses 29 to 32 give the heart of it: obey God rather than men, because God has raised and exalted Jesus.
basic.originalLanguages: The words sharpen the story. Ananias nosphizomai, kept back, secretly held part of the price, the same word used of Achan who kept back the devoted things at Jericho. Peter calls it a pseudomai, a lie, to the Holy Spirit. Before the council the apostles say they must peitharcheo, obey, God rather than men. And they proclaim that God exalted Jesus as archegos, Prince or Pioneer, and Savior, who grants repentance to Israel.
basic.typology: Ananias keeping back the devoted price recalls Achan, whose secret theft brought judgment into Israel, warning that hidden sin defiles God's people. The apostles freed from prison by an angel echo God's repeated rescues of His servants. Jesus exalted as Prince and Savior fulfills the promise of a ruler who leads His people to life, a new and greater Joshua and Moses combined.
basic.christ: The apostles' testimony centers on Jesus: the God of the fathers raised Him up after the leaders killed Him on a tree, and exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior to grant repentance and forgiveness to Israel. He is the living Lord whom they cannot stop preaching, and the good news they proclaim daily is simply that Jesus is the Christ. Even the judgment on Ananias guards the honor of His Spirit.
basic.god: God is holy and cannot be deceived; He sees the heart and will not let a lie sit unchallenged at the foundation of His church. He is also the God who saves, sending an angel to open the prison, exalting Jesus, and giving His Spirit to those who obey Him. He governs even the councils of His enemies, so that if this work is from God, no one can stop it.
basic.crossReferences: Joshua 7 tells of Achan keeping back the devoted things, the pattern behind Ananias. Deuteronomy 21:23 lies behind hanging on a tree. Acts 4:19-20 states the same resolve to obey God rather than men. Philippians 2:9-11 celebrates the God who exalted Jesus to the highest place.
basic.oneStory: The exalted Christ pours out His Spirit on a holy people, and God will keep that people true, even by fearful judgment, while He carries the gospel forward against every effort to silence it. Prison cannot hold His witnesses, threats cannot quiet them, and floggings only turn to joy. From Jerusalem the word keeps advancing, driven by the risen Prince and Savior toward the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
Luke has built Acts 5 as a mirror of Acts 4, and the reflections are deliberate. Acts 4:36 and 37 told of Barnabas, who sold a field and 'laid it at the apostles' feet.' Acts 5:1 to 11 tells of Ananias and Sapphira, who sold a piece of property and laid a portion 'at the apostles' feet.' Then a second arrest and a second appearance before the council, 5:17 to 40, repeat the first, 4:1 to 22, with every element raised a degree: the first time they were held overnight, now they are rescued from the jail; the first time they were warned, now they are flogged; the first time they went to their friends, now they leave rejoicing.

The scene of Ananias and Sapphira is tightly framed. 'Great fear came over all who heard,' verse 5, and again 'great fear came over the whole church and all who heard,' verse 11. In between, the story is told in two matched panels. The husband is confronted, dies and is buried; the wife enters unaware, is given a chance to tell the truth, lies, dies and is buried 'beside her husband.' Luke's first use of the word 'church' in Acts, in the best Greek text, falls in verse 11, so that the church is first named in the very verse that shows its holiness.

The summary of verses 12 to 16 is a hinge. It tells of wonders, crowds and the sick laid in the streets, and it makes a curious pair of statements: people held the believers in high esteem, yet no one dared to join them. The second half of the chapter then moves through a jailbreak told with comic irony. The council convenes to try men who are, at that moment, teaching in the temple. Gamaliel's speech is placed as a pause in the storm, and the chapter ends not on the flogging but on joy, and on the apostles teaching in the temple and in homes. Their last act matches what the angel commanded in verse 20, and so the chapter closes by showing obedience carried out to the end.
context.historical:
The community in Jerusalem was a growing body of believers living with a high degree of mutual dependence. Land was a family's main security, and those who sold it to feed others made a serious sacrifice. Public gifts brought public honour, which makes the sin of Ananias and Sapphira intelligible. They wanted the reputation of a Barnabas without paying for it. Their sin was not in keeping part of the price, as Peter says, but in pretending to give all.

The young men who carried out the bodies acted according to the custom that burial should be swift, in the same day or soon after. The absence of public mourning is part of Luke's picture of shock. Sapphira arrives about three hours later and has not been told, so there was no ordinary communication of the news; the church was in awe.

The council that tried the apostles was dominated by Sadducees, who, as Luke notes elsewhere, said there is 'neither a resurrection, nor angels, nor spirits,' Acts 23:8. It is a deliberate irony that men who denied angels have their prison opened by one. Gamaliel, by contrast, was a Pharisee and a teacher of high reputation, and Paul later says he was educated 'at the feet of Gamaliel,' Acts 22:3. His speech mentions two rebels. Judas the Galilean led a revolt at the time of the census, which Josephus places in AD 6. Theudas is harder: Josephus describes a Theudas who led a following to the Jordan under the governor Fadus, about a decade after Gamaliel's speech. Most explanations suppose an earlier rebel of the same name, since several uprisings followed the death of Herod the Great and Theudas was a common name, but the evidence is incomplete and a careful reader should say so.

Flogging was a recognised punishment. The law limited it to forty lashes, Deuteronomy 25:3, and in practice the count stopped at thirty-nine, which Paul recalls when he says he received 'the forty lashes minus one' five times, 2 Corinthians 11:24. It was painful and publicly shaming, and the apostles bear it in the city where they had been honoured.
context.canonical:
The death of Ananias and Sapphira stands in a line of judgments that fall at the beginning of a new stage in God's dealings. Achan took what was devoted to destruction when Israel entered the land, Joshua 7:1. Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorized fire at the start of the priesthood, Leviticus 10:1 to 3, and Moses' interpretation of that event is a key to this one: 'To those who come near Me I will show My holiness.' Uzzah touched the ark as it was brought toward Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 6:6 and 7. In each case a community newly drawn near to God is shown that nearness is dangerous to the careless. Luke's own verb for 'kept back,' in verses 2 and 3, is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses of Achan in Joshua 7:1.

The New Testament does not treat the event as a pattern of daily practice, but it does teach that the Lord disciplines His people. Paul says that some at Corinth have become weak, sick or have 'fallen asleep' because of abuse of the Lord's Supper, 1 Corinthians 11:30 to 32, and he calls the discipline a mercy so that they would not be condemned with the world. Hebrews warns that 'our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:29, and Revelation 2:23 says the risen Lord is the One who 'searches minds and hearts.'

The second half of the chapter belongs to the Bible's theme of the faithful witness. The principle of verse 29 has forerunners in the midwives who feared God, Exodus 1:17, and in Daniel's friends, Daniel 3:16 to 18. The joy of verse 41 follows Jesus' word, 'Rejoice in that day and leap for joy,' Luke 6:23, and is repeated in 1 Peter 4:13 and 14, where believers are told to rejoice as they share Christ's sufferings. The title 'Prince and Savior' in verse 31 uses the same Greek word as the 'Author of life' in Acts 3:15, and Hebrews 2:10 uses it again.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote the story of Ananias and Sapphira so that the church would never mistake grace for permission. The same chapter that celebrates open hands and a church growing in power also shows what God does with deceit at the heart of that church. He puts the two scenes side by side: Barnabas, whose gift was real, and a couple whose gift was theatre. Peter's question is not about money but about the heart: 'How could you conceive such a deed in your heart?'

The second half is written to strengthen the people who would suffer for the gospel. Luke shows the apostles arrested a second time, rescued, brought before the council, threatened with death and beaten, and he lets the reader see that they are not broken by it. He wants his readers to understand that obedience to God may cost them dearly, and that it is worth it. The line 'counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name' is the thing he most wants to be remembered.

He also seems to want his readers to hear Gamaliel with care. The wise counsel of a respected teacher saves the apostles' lives, and it is a reminder that God works through unlikely people and through rulers' own prudence. Yet Luke does not turn the rule into a doctrine. The apostles do not stop because a Pharisee said they might continue; they carry on because an angel told them to.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter reports two kinds of event. The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira and the miraculous release from prison are recorded as things that happened. Nothing in the text tells the church to look for divine executions or angelic jailbreaks, and the next chapters show other outcomes: Stephen is killed and not rescued, and James is put to the sword in Acts 12:2, while Peter in the same chapter is delivered. The record is of what God did, not of what he does on a schedule.

What carries forward has to be taken from what the text teaches. That God sees the heart and cannot be deceived, that lying to the church is lying to the Holy Spirit, that holy fear belongs to a healthy church, and that believers must obey God before men, are all principles that other Scripture confirms. The lesson on money is easily misread. Peter's words in verse 4 say that giving was never compelled, so the passage does not require every believer to give everything. It condemns the pretence.

Gamaliel's speech is also description. Luke records what he said, and it proved useful, but he does not say that every movement that survives is from God or that every persecuted one is false. The abiding instruction is in the apostles' reply of verse 29 and in their joy in verse 41, where the text itself speaks with God's voice.

debates.question: Is the sudden death of Ananias and Sapphira a pattern God will always follow, or a unique foundational judgment?

views.label: A unique, foundational sign, not the normal pattern
views.case: Like the judgment on Nadab and Abihu at the start of the priesthood or Achan at the entry to the land, this falls at the birth of the church to establish the holiness of the new community. Elsewhere the New Testament calls for church discipline and patient correction, not instant death, 1 Corinthians 5, Galatians 6:1; so the abiding lesson is the fearful seriousness of hypocrisy, not an expectation that liars will drop dead today.

views.label: A revealing window into how God always regards hypocrisy
views.case: The text says great fear came on the whole church, drawing a lasting lesson; God's holiness has not changed, and what is normally hidden is here made visible. Read this way, the passage warns every generation that lying to the Spirit is deadly serious, even when judgment is not immediate, lest the church presume on grace.

debates.bearing: Both readings hold that God is holy and takes hypocrisy with deadly seriousness; they differ on whether the immediate death is a repeatable pattern or a unique, founding sign whose enduring purpose is godly fear and honesty before God.

debates.question: Were Ananias and Sapphira true believers who were disciplined, or hypocrites who were never saved?

views.label: Unconverted pretenders
views.case: Peter says that Satan filled Ananias' heart, verse 3, language close to what Luke says of Judas, 'Satan entered Judas,' Luke 22:3. Luke does not call them disciples, and the narrator says that no one else dared join the believers after the event, verse 13. Like Achan, they are treated as an alien element exposed within the people of God. On this reading the passage shows that the church contains hypocrites and that God will expose them.

views.label: Believers under severe discipline
views.case: Others note that Peter does not say they were damned, and that Paul says some at Corinth were struck with sickness and death by the Lord's discipline 'so that we will not be condemned with the world,' 1 Corinthians 11:30 to 32. They point out that a believer can be deceived by Satan and fall into grave sin, as Peter himself did when he denied Jesus, and that judgment in this life does not settle a person's eternal state.

debates.bearing: The text does not tell us their final state, and neither view lessens the seriousness. Both hold that they sinned in a deliberate, calculated way against the Spirit within the church, that the discipline was God's, and that the rest of the church was taught to fear.

debates.question: Is Gamaliel's rule, that what is from God cannot be stopped, a reliable test of truth?

views.label: A sound principle that Luke affirms
views.case: Proverbs 21:30 says no counsel can prevail against the LORD, and the church did continue and grow despite every effort to stop it. Luke records Gamaliel's advice with evident approval, and the council yields to it. On this view the survival of the gospel in the face of opposition is itself a sign of its source.

views.label: A prudent counsel that cannot be made a general rule
views.case: Others observe that many false movements have lasted for centuries and that true prophets have often been killed, as Stephen will point out in Acts 7:52. Gamaliel is not an apostle and his speech is a piece of tactical wisdom spoken by a man who does not believe in Jesus. The test works in this case because God has already vindicated Jesus by the resurrection. It is not a rule for judging every case.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that God used Gamaliel to spare the apostles. The danger is to treat success or survival as the proof of truth. The apostles' own measure is the resurrection and the word of God, not numbers or longevity.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke tells us that Ananias 'kept back' some of the money, verse 2, using nosphizomai, a verb meaning to set aside for oneself, to pilfer. It is the verb that the Greek Old Testament uses of Achan in Joshua 7:1, who 'took some of what was set apart.' The same verb appears again in verse 3 of Peter's question. A reader steeped in Joshua would hear a second Achan at the start of a new conquest. The name Ananias is the Greek form of Hananiah, which means 'the LORD has been gracious,' a sad irony in a story about the abuse of grace.

Verses 3 and 4 move from 'lie to the Holy Spirit' to 'not lied to men, but to God.' The verb is pseudomai, to lie or deceive, and the two verses name its object first as the Holy Spirit and then as God. Peter treats them as one: to deceive the Spirit is to deceive God. The Spirit is not an impersonal force that can be tricked in the way a coin is spent, but a divine person who can be lied to and tested, as verse 9 repeats with 'test the Spirit of the Lord.' That verb, peirazo, is the verb of Deuteronomy 6:16, 'Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah.'

Peter's question in verse 4 has two parts that guard the human side of the sin. Satan 'filled your heart' in verse 3, but Peter also says, 'you have put this deed in your heart,' verse 4. The deed is both tempted and chosen. Verse 9 says the couple 'agreed together,' symphoneo, a word for harmony or concord. The church's own unity is described with 'one accord,' but here two people are in harmony to test the Spirit, a perverse version of the church's unity. The verb for 'died' in verses 5 and 10 is ekpsycho, to breathe out one's life, and Luke uses it again only of Herod in Acts 12:23, who also died after refusing to give glory to God.

When the council hears Peter's reply in verse 33, they are 'enraged,' diaprio, literally sawn through, cut to the quick. Luke uses the verb again of Stephen's hearers in Acts 7:54. The contrast with Acts 2:37 is the point. There the crowd was 'cut to the heart,' katanyssomai, and asked what to do; here the council is sawn through, and resolves to kill. The same message produces repentance in one hearer and murder in another.

Peter's twin verbs in verses 29 and 32 are the same. 'We must obey God,' verse 29, uses peitharcheo, which means to obey one in authority, from peitho and arche. The Spirit is given to those who 'obey' Him in verse 32, with the same word. The word 'must,' dei, again marks divine necessity. Obedience here is not a separate achievement but a faithful response to God's authority; Luke can say in Acts 6:7 that a great number of priests 'became obedient to the faith.' In verse 31 Jesus is archegos, 'Prince,' the same word as 'Author' in Acts 3:15, and 'Savior,' soter. God exalted Him 'to grant repentance,' so repentance is itself a gift, as in Acts 11:18.

Peter says Jesus was killed by 'hanging Him on a tree,' verse 30, using the word xylon, wood. It points to Deuteronomy 21:22 and 23, where anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse, and so to Galatians 3:13. Gamaliel warns that the council 'may even find yourselves fighting against God,' verse 39, using theomachoi, a word that Greek tragedy used of those who strive against a god. Verse 20 calls the message 'this new life,' literally 'the words of this Life,' a phrase that ties back to Jesus as the Author of life.

Verse 41 says the apostles were 'counted worthy,' katexioo, a rare verb of being deemed worthy, 'of suffering disgrace for the Name.' The final word is simply 'the Name,' with no further description, as devout Jews spoke of God, and as 3 John 7 does of the Christian mission. The verb for 'rejoicing,' chairo, and the infinitive 'to be dishonoured,' atimasthenai, put joy and shame together in one sentence. Finally, verse 42 says they 'did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news,' using euangelizo with didasko, the two verbs of teaching and gospel.

typology.type: Achan and the stolen devoted things, Joshua 7:1
typology.fulfillment: Israel had just crossed the Jordan and taken Jericho when Achan kept back some of what was devoted to God, and a whole people felt the loss, Joshua 7:11 and 12. The same shape appears at the start of the church: a new community, a holy gift and a secret keeping back, with Luke using Joshua's own verb. The escalation is that the hidden sin is now exposed by the Spirit through Peter, not by lot, and that the judgment falls on two persons, not on a family and flock. The type falls short in the mercy shown to the church afterward. Where Achor became a place of trouble, Hosea 2:15 says God turns the Valley of Achor into a 'gateway of hope.'

typology.type: Nadab and Abihu and the holy nearness of God, Leviticus 10:1-3
typology.fulfillment: At the inauguration of the priesthood two priests offered unauthorized fire, and fire from the LORD consumed them. Moses explained that those who come near God will see His holiness. The church is God's new dwelling, with a priesthood of all believers, 1 Peter 2:5 and 9, and the first scandal in that house is met with the same warning. The escalation is that the church is not a tent but a people in whom the Spirit lives. The correspondence is limited: the priests offered false worship, while Ananias offered false generosity, and Aaron's silence is matched by the church's fear, not by speech.

typology.type: The man hanged on a tree, Deuteronomy 21:22-23
typology.fulfillment: The law said that anyone hanged on a tree was under God's curse. Peter takes that phrase from the council's own mouth: 'You had killed by hanging Him on a tree,' and answers with the next sentence, 'God exalted Him.' Paul reads the curse as the heart of the cross, 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The correspondence is that the cursed man is the Saviour. The escalation is that the curse is borne for others, and the exaltation that follows is the proof that it was borne. The type does not describe anyone else, since no other hanged man was Prince and Savior.

typology.type: The Servant who offered His back, Isaiah 50:6
typology.fulfillment: The Servant in Isaiah says 'I offered My back to those who struck Me,' and does not hide from scorn. Jesus took such blows from the same council, and now His apostles are flogged by it. They go out rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for the Name. The correspondence is that the Servant's pattern is shared by His servants, John 15:20, Philippians 1:29. The escalation lies in the joy, which Jesus had commanded, Luke 6:23. The pattern falls short in that the apostles' suffering does not atone for anyone; only the Servant's does.

study.christ:
Peter's defence in verses 30 to 32 is a miniature of the gospel and every phrase is about Christ. 'The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree.' The first clause is the resurrection, the second the cross, and the phrase 'hanging on a tree' deliberately recalls the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23. Peter does not avoid the offence of the cross. He names it, and then answers it with what God did. 'God exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior.' Prince, archegos, is the leader who goes first and opens the way, and Savior is the one who rescues. He holds both offices by exaltation, so that the cursed man is also the sovereign.

The purpose of His exaltation is that He might 'grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel.' It is striking that the same hands that were stretched out on the cross are now stretched out to give. Christ does not merely accept repentance; He gives it. And He gives it first to the people who killed Him. The council hears an offer of forgiveness in the very words that indict them.

The risen Christ is also the Lord of His church in this chapter. The angel of the Lord opens the prison, and the commission to 'tell the people the full message of this new life' comes from Him. When Peter speaks to Ananias, the Spirit who rests on the church is discerning the heart, as Jesus Himself knew 'what was in a man,' John 2:25. The risen Lord says to the church at Thyatira that He is the One who 'searches minds and hearts,' Revelation 2:23. The holiness of the church in Acts 5 is Christ's own concern.

By contrast with Ananias, Christ is the one who held nothing back. He 'emptied Himself,' and 'became obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:7 and 8. Ananias kept a portion for himself and presented the rest as everything; Christ gave all and kept nothing, and then received everything as a gift from the Father.

The Name is the last link. The apostles rejoice 'for the Name,' a way of speaking that treats Jesus' name with the reverence that Israel gave to the name of God. And the closing sentence names the content of all their daily teaching: 'Jesus is the Christ.' The whole of Acts 5 hangs on the claim that the crucified man is God's Anointed.

As elsewhere, the guard against over-reading is the text. The jail, the shadow, the field and the money are not hidden pictures of Christ. The links lie where Peter himself puts them, in the tree, the exaltation, the Name and the Spirit's witness.
study.god:
The chapter begins with a God who sees. Peter knows what Ananias did before anyone has told him, and he explains it by saying that Ananias has lied to the Holy Spirit and so to God. The all-seeing God of the Psalms, who knows the heart, is present in the church. There is no hidden room in the assembly where His eyes do not reach, which is why the church is told to fear.

He is holy, and His holiness is not a mood but the settled character of His presence. The deaths are not an outburst but a demonstration, that God's nearness to His people is both the greatest gift and a fearful thing. 'Great fear' falls on the church, not despair. Hebrews says that 'our God is a consuming fire,' and urges worship 'with reverence and awe,' Hebrews 12:28 and 29. Paul writes, 'Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God,' Romans 11:22. Acts 5 offers the same lesson at the church's birth.

He is also the God who gives the Spirit, rescues, speaks and sustains. The angel's opening of the prison and the command to 'Go, stand in the temple courts' show a God who frees His witnesses to continue their work. But He does not always deliver. The apostles are flogged, and Stephen and James will be killed. The God of Acts 5 is the God who has a purpose for each of His servants, which sometimes includes rescue and sometimes does not, and who counts suffering for His name an honour.

He is sovereign over rulers. The council is enraged and wants to kill, and then it is turned aside by a Pharisee's measured speech. Proverbs 21:30 says no counsel can prevail against the LORD, and the chapter shows how: He can use a closed jail's emptiness, a rival party's wisdom, or the crowd's fear to keep His servants alive. He does not need to overthrow the council to protect His word.

He is the God who grants repentance. The exalted Christ gives repentance and forgiveness, verse 31, and the Spirit is given to those who obey, verse 32. God is both the one who commands and the one who enables the response.

For worship, the chapter calls for reverence and for joy. Reverence is the right response to a God who cannot be lied to, and joy is the right response to a God who counts His servants worthy to suffer for His name. The believers of Acts 5 learn that the God who can strike a lie dead is the same God who sends an angel to open a prison, and that both belong to the same holy love.

crossReferences.note: Achan took some of what was devoted to destruction and so brought the LORD's anger on all Israel. Luke's verb for Ananias 'keeping back,' in Acts 5:2, is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses here. Both stories fall at the start of a new stage in God's work, when the holiness of the community is being established.

Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorized fire at the start of the priesthood and died in the LORD's presence. Moses explained that God will show His holiness to those who come near Him. Acts 5 shows the same principle at the beginning of the church, God's new dwelling place, where nearness to Him is costly.

Barnabas sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. The story of Ananias and Sapphira is written as its shadow, with the same selling and the same laying at the feet, and so the true gift and the false gift are put side by side to show the difference of heart.

Moses told Israel not to test the LORD as they did at Massah. Peter says that Ananias and Sapphira agreed to 'test the Spirit of the Lord.' The couple's sin is cast in the light of Israel's wilderness history, where trifling with God's patience brought discipline, and it shows that the Spirit is the LORD who is not to be tested.

After Pilate washed his hands, the people cried, 'His blood be on us and on our children!' In Acts 5:28 the high priest says the apostles are determined to bring 'this man's blood' on the council. The council that once invited the responsibility now fears it, and does not name Jesus.

The law that anyone hanged on a tree is under God's curse. Peter says the council killed Jesus 'by hanging Him on a tree,' which points to the curse the cross carried. Paul explains in Galatians 3:13 that Christ became a curse for us, and Peter's next words show that God lifted the cursed man to His right hand.

An angel frees Peter from prison, though in the same chapter James has been executed. The pairing is a reminder that the deliverance in Acts 5 is one of God's ways and not His only one. God can open doors, and God can allow a martyrdom, and the church trusts Him in both.

Jesus tells His disciples to rejoice and leap for joy when people hate and insult them for the Son of Man's sake. The apostles who leave the Sanhedrin rejoicing in Acts 5:41 are carrying out that beatitude, and are doing so with the memory of their Master's words in their minds.

Paul says that some Corinthians are weak, sick or have fallen asleep because of how they came to the Lord's Supper, and that the Lord's judgment is discipline so that believers are not condemned with the world. The passage offers a lens for reading Acts 5 as a case of severe discipline within the church.

Luke notes that the Sadducees deny resurrection, angels and spirits, while the Pharisees acknowledge them all. In Acts 5 the Sadducean high priest's party arrests the apostles and an angel frees them. It is also a Pharisee, Gamaliel, who counsels restraint. Luke draws out the irony of each party's position.

No wisdom, understanding or counsel can prevail against the LORD. Gamaliel's warning that the council might find itself 'fighting against God' is a human restatement of this proverb, and the chapter shows it proved true in the way the church survived a series of attempts to stop it.

Paul recalls receiving five times the forty lashes minus one from the Jews. The apostles' flogging in Acts 5:40 belongs to the same punishment and shows what the church's mission would cost. Paul, who had studied under Gamaliel, Acts 22:3, counts it among the marks of his service.

Peter tells believers not to be surprised at the fiery trial and to rejoice in sharing the sufferings of Christ, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on them. He is repeating, for churches across the empire, the lesson that he and John learned in the council chamber.

Receiving an unshakable kingdom, believers are to worship with reverence and awe, since God is a consuming fire. It states in a sentence the response that Acts 5:11 records, great fear coming on the church, and sets that fear alongside gratitude.

study.oneStory:
The chapter belongs to the Bible's long argument about how a holy God can dwell among a sinful people. In Eden He walked with the man and woman, and sin sent them out. At Sinai He came down in fire, and the people could not approach, and the tabernacle was built with its curtains and priests to manage the distance. Each time God draws near to a people, He makes it clear that nearness has a cost: Nadab and Abihu at the tabernacle, Achan at Jericho, Uzzah at the ark. The question Acts 5 answers is what happens when God dwells not in a tent but in a people.

The answer is both severe and hopeful. The Spirit now lives in the church, and the church can be trusted with the presence of God only because Christ has made it holy. That is why the first sin inside the church is met at once, and why Luke can then say that no one dared to join them while still more believers were added to the Lord, verses 13 and 14. The community is a place of fear and of growth. The dwelling of God with human beings, which was lost in Genesis 3, is being rebuilt, and God means it to be kept clean.

The second half of the chapter looks forward to the story of persecution that runs through the rest of Acts and the New Testament. The council that opposed Jesus now opposes His church, and the pattern of arrest, trial, threat and growth will be repeated until Stephen's death scatters the believers, Acts 8:1, and the gospel moves outward as a result. The apostles' joy in suffering is the first sign of a church that will be tested and will not be broken.

The chapter ends with the apostles teaching and proclaiming that Jesus is the Christ in the temple and from house to house. This is the same message that the whole Old Testament was moving toward, that the Anointed One would suffer and enter His glory. In the new creation there will be no hypocrite, no council and no flogging. Revelation 21:27 says nothing unclean will enter the city, and Revelation 21:3 promises that God will dwell with His people. Acts 5 shows the church learning, in its first weeks, that the God who will live among them forever is holy, and that the way to Him lies through the Prince and Savior who was hanged on a tree and exalted to the right hand of God.

quiz.q: What was the real sin of Ananias and Sapphira?

options.text: They lied to the Holy Spirit, pretending to give everything while secretly keeping back part of the price.
options.note: Peter names it a lie to God and the Spirit; the hypocrisy, not the amount, was the sin.

options.text: They kept back some of the money from the sale of their land.
options.note: They did keep back part, but Peter stresses the land and proceeds were theirs to keep; the sin was the lie, not the reservation.

options.text: They refused to sell their property for the church.
options.note: They did sell it; the problem was pretending to give all while holding back, not refusing to give.

options.text: They gave too little compared with the other believers.
options.note: The size of the gift was never the issue; Peter says it remained at their disposal.

quiz.q: Why did great fear come over the whole church?

options.text: Because God had shown, in the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira, that He will not be lied to or trifled with.
options.note: Verse 11 links the fear to God's holy judgment on the deceit.

options.text: Because two members of the church had suddenly died.
options.note: The deaths caused the fear, but the deeper cause was recognizing God's holiness and the seriousness of lying to Him.

options.text: Because the authorities were about to arrest everyone.
options.note: The fear arose from God's judgment within the church, not from the authorities at this point.

options.text: Because the apostles had lost their healing power.
options.note: The apostles went on to heal many; there was no loss of power.

quiz.q: How did the apostles answer the council's order to stop teaching in Jesus' name?

options.text: They said they must obey God rather than men, and testified that God raised and exalted Jesus.
options.note: Verses 29 to 32 give both the principle and the testimony.

options.text: They declared that they were witnesses of these things, along with the Holy Spirit.
options.note: True, from verse 32, but the governing answer is the principle that they must obey God rather than men.

options.text: They promised to teach only in private from house to house.
options.note: They kept teaching both in the temple and house to house; they made no such compromise.

options.text: They fell silent out of fear of the high priest.
options.note: They did the opposite, refusing to be silenced and rejoicing to suffer.

quiz.q: How does Peter describe what God has done with the crucified Jesus?

options.text: God exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, to grant repentance and forgiveness to Israel.
options.note: Verse 31 states His exaltation and saving purpose.

options.text: God raised Him up after the leaders had killed Him on a tree.
options.note: True, from verse 30, but the fuller statement adds His exaltation as Prince and Savior granting repentance.

options.text: God appointed Him as a teacher whose example we should follow.
options.note: He is far more than an example; He is the exalted Prince and Savior who grants repentance and forgiveness.

options.text: God has left His future reign uncertain until Israel repents.
options.note: Peter proclaims Him already exalted at God's right hand, not waiting to be enthroned.

quiz.q: What was the substance of Gamaliel's counsel to the Sanhedrin?

options.text: Leave these men alone, for if their work is from God you cannot stop it, and you may be fighting against God.
options.note: Verses 38 to 39 capture his argument from precedent to caution.

options.text: Recall how Theudas and Judas the Galilean rose and came to nothing.
options.note: He cited these examples, but as support for his conclusion to let the apostles go.

options.text: Release the apostles because they had done nothing wrong at all.
options.note: Gamaliel argued from prudence and providence, not from a verdict of innocence; they were still flogged.

options.text: Put the apostles to death at once to end the movement.
options.note: That was the council's first impulse, which Gamaliel argued against.

quiz.q: How did the apostles respond to being flogged and released?

options.text: They rejoiced to be counted worthy of suffering for the Name and kept proclaiming that Jesus is the Christ.
options.note: Verses 41 to 42 show their joy and their unbroken witness.

options.text: They kept teaching daily in the temple and from house to house.
options.note: True, from verse 42, but it omits the striking note that they rejoiced to suffer disgrace for the Name.

options.text: They obeyed the order and stopped speaking for a while.
options.note: They did not stop; they continued teaching every day despite the order.

options.text: They grew discouraged and scattered from Jerusalem.
options.note: They were joyful and steadfast, not discouraged, and remained proclaiming Christ.

questions: Ananias and Sapphira wanted the reputation of total devotion without its reality. Where are you tempted to appear more surrendered to God than you truly are, and what would honesty before Him look like?
Peter said the couple had lied not to men but to God. How does remembering that God sees the heart change the way you approach your giving, your words, and your worship?
The apostles said they must obey God rather than men. Where might your loyalty to Christ come into conflict with a human expectation or authority, and how will you decide?
God exalted Jesus as Prince and Savior to grant repentance. Is there an area where you need to receive His gift of repentance rather than manage your sin on your own?
An angel opened the prison, yet the apostles were still flogged soon after. How do you hold together God's power to rescue and His call to endure suffering for the Name?
The apostles left the council rejoicing to have suffered for Jesus. What would it take for you to count opposition for Christ as an honor rather than merely a burden?

translationNotes.note: The verb rendered kept back means to secretly set apart for oneself or embezzle; the Greek Old Testament uses the same word of Achan in Joshua 7:1, drawing a pointed parallel.
Sanhedrin can be rendered the Council, here described further as the full assembly of the elders of Israel.
Hanging Him on a tree draws on Deuteronomy 21:22-23; the language marks Jesus' death as bearing a curse, which Paul unfolds in Galatians 3:13.
Prince translates Archegos, which can also be rendered Leader, Author, or Pioneer; it pictures Christ as the one who goes first and opens the way of life for His people.
